questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to improve my German and travel in a climate friendly manner. Furthermore, previous exchange students had written in their reports that the administration at the university in Mannheim was great, which was important to me, because I did not want to stress over administrative issues (unfortunately this was not my experience).

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The score is not that high, because I was a bit unlucky and experienced some extraordinary challenges and events in the city and at the university. However, I also had many good experiences and most exchange students have a great time in Mannheim.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy - the university provides detailed guides.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: My buddy (a student) and contact information on the international office at the university

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Quite easy, but maybe I was lucky, because there are many students, who apply. If you want your accomodation to be social, I would recommend looking on
www.wg-gesucht.de
.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If you live in the inner city ("Quadrate"), Jungbusch or "the Horseshoe" (the ring around the inner city), you will be close to eveything.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Registration for the intranet and enrollment was easy - the university gives you thorough guidance. Registering for courses is another story, though... 

We had to "pre-register" before the exchange and then register officially later. For the final registration the IT system was down for most of the registration period and the faculty had changed the course schedules completely without notice, meaning that multiple of my courses were suddenly overlapping. The faculty was unreachable (by mail, phone and in person), when I tried to solve the problem.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Guides and personel (in principle)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very successful - 2/5 of my courses I was "forced" to take due to schedulling issue

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
1) make sure to check that none of your courses overlap both when pre-registering and for the final registration. Be prepared that the schedule might change even after you have made sure that everything works out. 

2) get more courses pre-approved than you need, so you can adjust to changing schedules.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The academic programme is generally well put together, but there was one course that was so chaotic, useless and even misleading that I found it unfair to students to offer it. 

Notably, they have a more laissez-faire attitude towards exams (the supervisor would show up 5 minutes before the exam and there would be a loud conference going on in the neighbouring corridor). So the conditions for taking exams are not always ideal.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is lower than at UCPH and you do not have to prepare much, because the curriculum is the PowerPoint slides that are used in class.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is similar - the professor will do a presentation and sometimes the students will do small cases/exercises. However, there are no mock exams and previous exams are often not made available to students.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Advocacy Skills (6 ETCS - oral exam), International Civil and Commercial Litigation (8 ECTS - 2 hour take-at-home exam), International Sale of Goods (6 ECTS - 1 hour written exam), International Trade Law (6 ETCS - 1 hour written exam), Law & Economics (& ETCS - 1 hour written exam).

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Advocacy skills: the professor is entertaining and the course provides useful insights on how basic communication techniques can improve your legal practice. The exam is quite relaxed. 

Law & Economics: an interesting course that gives you a sense of how the law and legal issues are analysed from an economic point of view. You have to put some work into it, though, because you have to know all the economic theories by heart at the exam. 

DO NOT TAKE INTENATIONAL TRADE LAW: it was a chaotic and pointless presentation of cases from a local law firm. The lawyers, who were teaching, answered the questions for the class themselves, because none of the students understood what the point was.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: A semester fee around 900 DKK

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Living costs in Germany are lower than in Copenhagen and you get student discounts more often.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The ESN VISUM makes a lot of events for exchange students and there are many student-driven clubs. Furthermore, a gym membership is relatively cheap and there are different sports teams/classes offered.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Events by ESN VISUM Mannheim, because it is a great way to meet people and it is fun. 

I also recommend the International Summer/Winter Academy (an intensive German course offered by the university). You have to pay for it, but you meet exchange students from alle over the world and you get time to settle in to life in Mannheim, before the semester starts.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Heidelberg, when it is sunny - it is prettier than Mannheim and a nice get-away. Smaller cities, such as Worms, Speyer and Schwetzingen are also worth a visit. 

If you get the chance to go to Faschingskarneval in Cologne or Oktober-/Frühlingsfest in Stuttgart, you should go - it is a lot of fun. 

You will get plenty of opportunities to travel across Germany and Europe, because many exchange students from e.g. the US, Asia and Australia want to see as much of Europe as possible and Mannheim is a great starting point due to its central location.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy, but remember to have cash and do not expect IT systems to live up to Danish standards.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Find a WG room or join a student club/sports team

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Social and economic differences are more obvious than in Denmark, so there are more people living on/wandering around the streets and crime is a bigger issue than back home. 

I got catcalled way more than in Copenhagen and had some unpleasant experiences, so I had to think more about how I got home at night than I normally do.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: (most) Sounthern German people are warm-hearted and like to small talk. People can afford going to cafes and restaurants and do it often.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Join ESN VISUM events and the International Summer or Winter Academy
2) The courses are not as demanding as at home, but even if you study throughout the semester, the exams might be challenging because they are conducted very differently from what we are used to
3) You will not have that much control over which courses and exams you end up taking.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring and old-fashioned wrist-watch because there are no clocks in the examination rooms

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Improving my German and experiencing living in another country

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Administrative issues throughout the semester, exams and safety.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
